name: docker
one_line: build and run containers (isolated, packaged applications)
plain: A container is a lightweight, isolated box that holds a program and everything it needs. An image is the packaged recipe; a container is a running copy of an image. `docker` is the command that builds images and runs containers.
Labs love it: one command starts a vulnerable machine, another deletes it, so your computer stays clean. This page is focused on the most-used commands, not every option.
Security note: being in the docker group (or being able to run docker) is almost the same as being root on that host, because you can mount the host's folders into a container.
when: Start a ready-made lab or tool (DVWA, Juice Shop, a Kali image).
Run a command in an isolated environment.
Build your own image from a Dockerfile.
Copy files in and out of a container.
Clean up unused containers and images.

examples.title: Run a container and get a shell
examples.explain: -it gives an interactive terminal, --rm deletes the container when you exit. You are now in a fresh Ubuntu.

examples.title: Run a web lab in the background
examples.explain: -d detaches, --name names it, -p 3000:3000 maps your port 3000 to the container's port 3000. Browse to http://localhost:3000.

examples.title: What is running?
examples.explain: ps lists running containers; -a includes stopped ones.

examples.title: Get a shell in a running container
examples.explain: exec runs a command inside an existing container; sh because many small images lack bash.

examples.title: Stop and remove
examples.cmd:
docker stop juice
docker rm juice
examples.explain: stop ends it politely, rm deletes the container. docker rm -f does both.

examples.title: Share a folder with the container
examples.explain: -v host:container mounts your current folder at /work, -w sets the starting folder. Edits are visible on both sides.

examples.title: Build an image
examples.explain: Reads the Dockerfile in the current folder and tags the result myimage.

examples.title: Copy files
examples.cmd:
docker cp juice:/etc/hosts ./hosts
docker cp ./note.txt juice:/tmp/
examples.explain: cp moves files between your machine and a container.

examples.title: Inspect and tidy
examples.cmd:
docker inspect juice | head -40
docker image ls
docker system prune
examples.explain: inspect prints settings and IP; image ls lists images; system prune removes unused containers, networks and dangling images (it asks first).

examples.title: Compose several containers
examples.cmd:
docker compose up -d
docker compose down
examples.explain: A docker-compose.yml describes a multi-container lab; up -d starts it, down removes it.

options.plain: -i keep input open, -t give a terminal.

Help for any command: docker run --help.

mistakes: Forgetting --rm and filling the disk with stopped containers.
Exposing a lab to the world with -p 0.0.0.0: use 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 for local-only.
Expecting data to survive: container storage is deleted with the container unless you mount a volume.
Using --privileged or mounting / without understanding that it hands over the host.
Running docker without sudo and getting 'permission denied': add your user to the docker group (which is itself a privilege decision).
Using :latest and getting a different image later.
try: Run ubuntu with -it --rm and check cat /etc/os-release.
Start Juice Shop on port 3000 and stop it again.
Mount your current folder into a container and create a file from inside.
Run docker system df to see what takes space.

captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
